The sides of a square are increasing in length at a rate of $3\text{ mm/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square changing when the sides have a length of $12\text{ mm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of $3\,\text{mm/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3.$ Also, when the sides are $12\,\text{mm},$ we have $x=12.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =3\cdot 2(12)=72{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square increases at $72\,{\text{mm}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

questions.problem: The sides (in feet) of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to four times the rate of increase of the diagonals. What is the length of the diagonals of the square at that moment?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$, so replacing $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 4\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 4 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have that the length of the diagonals of the square is $4\text{ feet}.$

canonical_examples.problem: The sides of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to twice the rate of increase of the diagonal. What is the area of the square at that moment?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

Using implicit differentiation and the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 2\dfrac{\textrm d h}{\textrm d t}$, so replacing $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm dt}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 2\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 2 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have $h=2,$ and therefore the area of the square at that moment is

$$
A = \dfrac{2^2}{2} = 2.
$$

tutorials.problem:
Suppose that the lengths of the sides of a square are growing at a **rate** of $2\,\textrm{cm}$ every second, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14210206/assets/6e791c7c33636ef3b2b798fde58825cf4cf1f76e3b6abdd2d92317aa555e1420.png)

If the square is growing, then its area is also increasing. Our question is, "*what is the rate at which the area of the square is increasing*?" In other words, if $A$ is the area of the square at time $t$, then what is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}?
$$

Let $x$ be the length of the side of the square. We know that the relationship between the area $A$ and side length $x$ is given by

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $x$ grows at a **rate** of $2\,\textrm{cm/s},$ so we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} = 2.
$$

Substituting the above into our expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t},$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 2 \cdot 2x =4x.
$$

And that's it. We're done!

If we want to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}$ at a particular moment, we substitute the value of $x$ at that moment into the above.

For example, to work out the rate of change of area when $t=2$ seconds, we substitute the corresponding value of $x$ into the formula. When $t=2$ we have $x=4$ (from the diagram) and therefore

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 4(4) = 16\,\textrm{cm}^2/\textrm{s}.
$$

tutorials.problem:
Suppose that the rate of change of the diagonal of a square is known, and we're interested in finding the rate of change of some other quantity. For example, can we calculate the rate of change of the area of a square given the rate of change of its diagonal?

Before we get into that, let's recall a few facts about squares. Consider the square $ABCD$ with sides of length $x$ and diagonals of length $h.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14210206/assets/0cc3f0cd81cae3bab92ec6c3826f64b7e54e0af61cc32a000569afe5171a27dc.png)

Using the Pythagorean Theorem, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & ={h}^{2} \\ 2{x}^{2} & ={h}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the area $A$ of a square is given by $A = x^2.$ So, since $x^2 = \dfrac{h^2}{2},$ we have

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

This formula will prove particularly handy in the next example.
